oneLineAnswer: Azelastine is an antihistamine nose spray and eye drop that eases sneezing, runny nose and itchy eyes from allergies.
whatItIs: Azelastine is an antihistamine medicine. Histamine is the chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction. Azelastine blocks the histamine receptor called H1, so labels call it an H1-receptor antagonist. In the United States it comes as a nose spray and as eye drops. Some nose sprays need a prescription, and one spray is sold over the counter.
whatItDoes: The prescription nose spray is approved for seasonal allergic rhinitis, the hay fever pattern of sneezing and a runny nose.
It is also approved for vasomotor rhinitis, a runny nose that is not caused by allergy.
The eye drops are approved for itchy eyes from allergic conjunctivitis, the eye reaction that comes with allergies.
Labels describe the drug as blocking histamine and calming mast cells, the cells that release histamine.
In a challenge study, the drops began easing itch within about 3 minutes and worked for about 8 hours.
howPeopleUseIt: The nose spray is only for the nose, and labels say not to spray it in the eyes or mouth.
Labels record a set number of sprays or drops per day, taken in one or two sessions.
Some people spray with the head tilted down, because the label says this helps with the bitter taste.
Soft contact lens wearers are told to wait about 10 minutes after the drops before reinserting lenses.
Labels say not to share the nose spray bottle, to avoid spreading germs.

commonSideEffects: Bitter taste is the most common complaint with the nose spray, reported by about 1 in 5 people at the higher dose.
Headache was next, at roughly 15% of people in the same trials.
Sleepiness was reported by about 12% of people at that dose.
Nose burning, nosebleeds, sore throat and dry mouth were also reported, each in a few people out of 100.
With the eye drops, burning or stinging on use was the most common complaint, at about 30%.
seriousSigns: The prescription label warns that sleepiness can happen, so driving or running machines needs care.
The over-the-counter label says to stop use and ask a doctor if a skin rash or other allergic reaction appears.
The same label says to stop and ask a doctor about severe or frequent nosebleeds.
The eye drops are for the eyes only and must not be swallowed or injected.
whoShouldAvoid: Do not use the nose spray if you have ever had an allergic reaction to it or to any ingredient in it.
The eye drops are not for anyone with a known or suspected allergy to their ingredients.
Ask a doctor first if you have had recent nose ulcers or nose surgery, or a nose injury that has not healed.
The over-the-counter spray is not for children under 6 years.
Avoid alcohol and other sedating medicines while using the nose spray, because alertness can drop further.

interactions: The nose spray label says to avoid alcohol and other central nervous system depressants, because alertness and thinking can suffer more.
The over-the-counter label names alcohol, sedatives and tranquilizers as things that can increase drowsiness.
pregnancyAndChildren: The nose spray label says decades of use in pregnancy have not shown risks of miscarriage or birth defects. It describes that data as limited. Animal studies at very high oral doses did show fetal harm. The label says there are no data on azelastine in human milk. It suggests watching a breastfed baby for signs of milk rejection, because the drug tastes bitter. The prescription nose spray is approved for seasonal allergic rhinitis from age 5. It is approved for vasomotor rhinitis from age 12. The eye drops are for age 3 and older. The over-the-counter spray says not for children under 6. Its label says to ask a health professional first if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.
whatWeDoNotKnow: There are no published data on how much azelastine reaches human milk.
Labels note that side-effect rates from one drug's trials cannot be compared with another drug's.
The exact liver enzymes that break azelastine down are not known.
The effect of race on how the body handles azelastine has not been studied.
Trial safety data in the labels cover days to weeks, so long-term effects are less clear.
This record does not cover how much anyone should use.

gaps: NCCIH has no azelastine page: https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/azelastine returned 404, so no NCCIH citation appears here.

MedlinePlus drug monograph pages are copyrighted (American Society of Health-System Pharmacists) and were neither fetched nor cited. The MedlinePlus allergy health topic was used only to confirm the drug monograph rule, not as evidence.
The PubChem endpoint that combines physchem properties with a Description returned HTTP 400 Bad Request, so identity facts come from the property endpoint alone.
NCCIH's allergy page rendered as stylesheet text on fetch, so it contributed no usable sentence for evidence.
The label facts rest on openFDA label records, with DailyMed, PubChem and ClinicalTrials.gov as separate confirming publishers. Several of these are U.S. federal sources.
No human milk quantity data, no head-to-head comparison against other antihistamines, and no long-term safety data beyond weeks were found.
No product-specific dose amounts were recorded here on purpose, even though labels state them.
Nothing in the fetched sources covers azelastine use in children below the approved ages for each form.
summary: This record covers what azelastine is, its nasal spray and eye drop forms, the label-recorded benefits and side effects, its warnings and interactions, pregnancy and child age limits, and the gaps in the sources checked.
